lessons.title: Case Study: Fixing a Working Capital Crunch in an Indian Manufacturer

children.text: This last lesson puts the whole course to work on one business. Ashwin Engineering Ltd machines pump and valve components in Coimbatore for three large original equipment manufacturers and about ninety smaller customers. FY2026 sales were ₹240 crore, up 18%, at an operating margin of 11%. The order book is full and the company has never made a loss.

It also could not pay salaries on time in February, its cash credit limit is 97.8% drawn, and two suppliers have stopped delivering on credit. Work through the diagnosis and the fix in the order a competent finance head would.

cells: Inventory plus receivable minus payable days

children.text: Three numbers explain the crisis. The company funds 113.4 days of its own operations. Its payable days of 139.9 are far beyond the 45 days agreed with most suppliers, which is why two of them have stopped supplying on credit. And with the limit 97.8% drawn, there is no buffer left for a bad week.

body.text: Note what a cash conversion cycle of 113.4 days means at this scale. One day of sales is about ₹0.66 crore, so the cycle ties up roughly ₹74.6 crore. The business is profitable and structurally short of cash at the same time, which is exactly the condition Chapter 1 opened with.

children.text: Step Two: Open the Three Lines
Totals diagnose nothing. Here is what sits inside them.

stats.label: Receivables over 90 days
stats.context: 15.4% of the book, against agreed terms of 45 to 60 days

stats.label: Non-moving inventory
stats.context: 14.5% of stock with no issue in twelve months

stats.label: Overdue MSME dues
stats.context: Of ₹17 crore owed to registered micro and small suppliers, accruing statutory interest

children.text: The last line is the most urgent, and not for commercial reasons. Under the MSMED Act, ₹11 crore beyond 45 days is accruing interest at three times the bank rate, compounded monthly, and any amount still unpaid on 31 March will be disallowed for tax. The company has been treating its most legally protected suppliers as its cheapest source of funding.

body.title: Where would you start?
body.question: You have limited management attention for the first fortnight. Which of these should come first?
options: Renegotiating credit terms with all ninety smaller customers
Clearing the overdue MSME dues and disposing of the non-moving inventory
Asking the bank for a limit enhancement
Introducing an inventory management system across all stock keeping units
body.explanation: The MSME dues are accruing punitive statutory interest and a tax disallowance, so delay has a measurable cost per day. The non-moving stock is cash already spent that can be partly recovered without negotiating with anyone. Both are within the company's own control. A limit enhancement takes weeks and is a far easier conversation once the first two are underway, and a systems project helps next year, not this fortnight.

children.text: Six actions, each with an owner, a target and a number. Nothing here requires a new product, a price increase or fresh equity.

cells: Collections discipline: named owner per customer, weekly ageing review, dispatch stop at 30 days past due
Discount invoices of the three large buyers on a TReDS platform
Convert ₹19.7 crore of exposure into cash within days
Dispose non-moving stock: use, return, sell or scrap, item by item
ABC and VED classification, reorder levels reset on class A items
Pay MSME suppliers within 45 days, negotiate 60-day terms with two large non-MSME vendors
Payable days to about 120, legally clean
Carve the permanent layer into a working capital demand loan and seek a limit enhancement
Restore headroom on the cash credit limit

body.text: Look at the fifth row. Paying suppliers properly costs ₹6.5 crore of cash, and it is still the right call. It stops the statutory interest, removes the tax disallowance, restores two supply relationships, and takes the company out of a funding source it has no legal right to use. Not every working capital action releases cash, and a plan that only contains the ones that do is not a plan.

body.title: Size one action
body.prompt: Ashwin Engineering wants to cut receivable days by 20 on sales of ₹240 crore. How much cash does that release, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: One day of sales is ₹240 crore divided by 365, about ₹0.66 crore. Twenty days releases roughly ₹13.2 crore. Every collections meeting in the company should know this number, because it converts a process discussion into a cash target.

events.title: Stop the bleeding
events.description: Clear overdue MSME dues in order of size and age. List every non-moving item with a decision against it. Tell the bank what you are doing before it asks.

events.title: Install the discipline
events.description: Named collections owner per customer, weekly ageing review with sales and finance together, and the dispatch stop at 30 days past due written into the system rather than the policy.

events.title: Open the cheaper funding
events.description: Onboard the three large buyers onto a TReDS platform and start discounting. Reset reorder levels on class A items using actual usage data.

events.title: Restructure the funding
events.description: Take the projections to the bank: carve the permanent layer into a demand loan, seek an enhancement, and use the released cash to cut the drawn balance rather than to fund more credit.

events.title: Hold the gains
events.description: Monthly cross-functional review, sales incentives moved from booking to collection, and a quarterly non-moving stock review so the ₹9 crore does not rebuild.

children.text: Step Four: What It Adds Up To

body.caption: The position after twelve months (₹ crore)

cells: Cash used to pay suppliers properly

body.label: What the year bought
body.context: Interest saving of about ₹2.19 crore a year at 10.75%, plus ₹0.38 crore from cheaper funding on the large buyers, with the cash credit limit back to 52.4% utilised and headroom restored.

children.text: Put the interest saving next to the profit line to see why this matters. The company earns ₹26.4 crore of operating profit. The working capital programme adds roughly ₹2.57 crore to the bottom line with no new sales, and it returns ₹20.4 crore of cash that was already inside the business. Neither number required a single rupee of new capital.

body.title: What the plan deliberately did not do

children.text: It did not cut credit terms across the board. Ninety smaller customers on tighter terms would have cost volume, and the receivables problem was concentrated in ageing and collection discipline rather than in the terms themselves. The dispatch stop does more than a policy change would.

It did not stretch suppliers further. That was the existing strategy, it had already cost two supply relationships and was accruing statutory interest, and it was the reason the company thought it was solvent when it was not.

It did not start with a limit enhancement. A bank asked for more money by a company with 15.4% of its receivables over 90 days and 14.5% of its stock non-moving will ask about both before discussing the amount. The same request three months into a visible programme is a different conversation.

It did not attempt a systems implementation in year one. Reorder levels on class A items, computed in a spreadsheet from actual usage, captured most of the inventory gain. The system can follow once the discipline exists, since software applied to an undisciplined process produces faster chaos.

body.title: The board pushes back
body.scenario: You present the plan. The managing director accepts the inventory and collections actions but objects to two things. First, he does not want a dispatch stop at 30 days past due, because the sales head says three mid-sized customers will go to a competitor. Second, he wants to keep stretching the MSME suppliers for another two quarters, since "they have never charged us interest in fifteen years". He also asks why, if the plan releases ₹20 crore, the company still needs to talk to the bank.
body.prompt: How would you answer all three points?
body.modelAnswer:
Answer each with a number rather than a principle.

On the dispatch stop: agree a narrower version rather than defending the original. Apply the automatic stop at 45 days past due instead of 30 for existing customers with a clean two-year record, and at 30 days for everyone else, with any override requiring the managing director's own written approval. That preserves the discipline while giving the sales head room on the three accounts he is worried about, and it puts the exception on the desk of the person who wants it. Then show what those three customers actually cost: if they are carrying, say, ₹6 crore at 120 days against agreed 60, then half that balance is excess, and funding it costs about ₹32 lakh a year at the company's own borrowing rate. That is the price of keeping them on current behaviour.

On the MSME suppliers: this is not a commercial judgement and it should not be presented as one. Interest accrues automatically under the statute whether or not the supplier claims it, the claim survives long after the relationship ends, and any amount unpaid beyond the limit on 31 March is disallowed for tax, so the company pays tax now on money it still owes. On ₹11 crore overdue, the tax cost alone is meaningful, and the interest is not deductible. Fifteen years of forbearance is evidence about those suppliers, not about the law.

On why the bank conversation still matters: because ₹20 crore released over twelve months does not arrive on day one, and growth consumes part of it as it arrives. At 15% growth, the business needs roughly ₹8 crore of additional working capital next year even at the improved cycle. The plan takes the company from no headroom to real headroom, and the restructuring of the permanent layer into a demand loan is what stops the same crisis recurring. Going to the bank from a position of visible improvement is also how the company gets better terms, which is worth more than going later from a position of strain.

body.title: The two ways this story usually ends

columns.label: The company that only cuts
points: Collections tighten, inventory falls, cash is released
The released cash funds longer credit to win more volume
The cycle drifts back within eighteen months
The same board meeting happens again with bigger numbers
Nobody owns the cycle, so nobody notices the drift

columns.label: The company that changes how it runs
points: The same actions, plus a monthly cross-functional review
Sales incentives paid on collection rather than booking
A named owner for each of the three working capital lines
Quarterly non-moving stock review with a decision on every item
A cycle target in the annual plan, alongside the sales target

body.title: The action that costs cash
body.textWithBlank: Paying overdue micro and small suppliers within the statutory limit uses cash rather than releasing it, but it stops the ___ interest accruing at three times the bank rate and removes the tax disallowance.
body.explanation: Not every working capital action releases cash. Paying protected suppliers on time costs ₹6.5 crore here and is still among the highest-return decisions in the plan.

body.title: The playbook, in the order it should be run
steps: Compute the three day-counts and the cycle, and convert the cycle into rupees using daily sales.
Open the receivables ageing, the inventory issue register and the payables list, and identify what is legally protected.
Clear anything accruing statutory interest or a tax disallowance first, since delay there has a measurable daily cost.
Dispose of non-moving stock item by item, because it is cash already spent and needs no negotiation.
Install collections discipline with named owners, weekly ageing reviews and an automatic dispatch stop.
Move large-buyer invoices to cheaper funding through TReDS or bill discounting.
Reset order quantities and reorder levels on class A items using actual usage data.
Restructure the funding: carve the permanent layer into a term facility, and seek an enhancement once the programme is visible.
Change what people are measured on, or the cycle rebuilds within two years.
Review the three lines monthly with sales, procurement, operations and finance in the same room.

body.title: The whole course in seven ideas

cards.definition: A business pays for inputs before it collects from customers, and that timing gap is what creates the need for working capital.
Converting every line into days lets you compare any two businesses, and multiplying days by daily sales converts them back into cash.
Inventory, receivable and payable days tell three different stories, and the net cycle can hide deterioration in all three.
How much to hold and how to fund it are two separate decisions, and the permanent layer should never sit on a demand facility.
The ageing schedule, not the total or the average, is where the risk and the loss actually live.
Supplier credit is never free, and for registered micro and small suppliers the price is set by statute, not by negotiation.

cards.term: Cash released is worth more than profit earned
cards.definition: It arrives immediately, needs no new sales, lowers the capital employed and raises the self-funded growth rate.

body.text: Working capital crises are never solved by a single dramatic action. They are solved by six ordinary ones, each with a named owner and a number, run for a year, and then kept running so the problem does not quietly rebuild.

points: Diagnose before acting: compute the three day-counts, convert the cycle into rupees, then open the ageing schedule, the issue register and the payables list.
Start with anything accruing statutory interest or a tax disallowance, because the cost of delay there is measurable and daily.
Non-moving stock is the fastest release, since it is cash already spent and requires no negotiation with anyone.
Collections discipline works through named owners and an automatic dispatch stop, not through tighter terms for everyone.
Some correct actions consume cash, such as paying protected suppliers properly, and a credible plan contains them.
In this case, ₹20.4 crore was released and the cycle cut by 28.4 days, adding about ₹2.57 crore to profit with no new sales and no new capital.
Without changed incentives and a monthly cross-functional review, the cycle rebuilds within about two years and the same meeting happens again.
